Marguerite found the book where she always did on Thursdays: wedged between the flour bins and the cooling racks, as if it had climbed in through the wall. *A Field Guide to Coastal Birds*, spine cracked, a faded library stamp inside the cover. Due date long past.

Eleven Thursdays now. She'd asked the day staff, checked the locks, even stayed late once with a thermos and a rolling pin. Nothing. The book simply appeared between two and four a.m., and she never caught the moment.

Tonight it was heavier. She opened it and a folded square of receipt paper slid out.

*I keep meaning to bring it back to the library, but I walk past your window on the way and the light is on, and I think: somebody is awake. Then I leave it here instead. Sorry. I'll stop if you ask me to.*

Marguerite read it twice. Behind her the ovens ticked, and the first trays of rye waited under their cloths.

She turned the receipt over, found a pencil stub behind her ear, and wrote on the back: *Don't stop.* Then she tucked it inside the cover, set the book on the sill by the front window, and left the light on.

I’ve been going to Vegas pretty much my whole life—well, the under-21 version of it—so I’ve sat through a lot of shows before I could even gamble. Le Rêve at the Wynn is one I finally caught, and honestly? Mixed. Maybe slightly worse than mixed.

First, the good: the circular stage is genuinely smart. You’re basically looking down into it, so from essentially any seat you get a decent view. That’s rare in Vegas. Some individual acts are impressive too—the strength stuff, the aerialists, the divers. Those people are athletes, no question. But a lot of it reminded me of Cirque du Soleil. Not in a “rip-off” way exactly, just... if you’ve seen Cirque, you’ve seen comparable feats done with maybe more clarity.

And clarity is the problem. What is the story? I still don’t know. There’s a dream, maybe? A guy? Water? It felt like a bunch of pretty images thrown at you, and the show never tells you what it’s trying to say. Also, there’s way too much happening at once. Too many people, too many elements, too many “wow” moments stacked on top of each other. A more restrained production would hit harder. This felt like the stereotypical Vegas spectacle thing—more must be better—so they crammed everything in.

Ticket note: if you’re staying at Wynn or Encore, they have a deal—$99 instead of the normal $125. That helps. Would I see it again? Probably not, and I wouldn’t pay for it a second time. Apart from a few stunts, it was just average. I wasn’t blown away, and I don’t think anyone else was either. That said, a few friends liked it, and if you’ve never seen it, maybe check it out. Just don’t expect to leave overwhelmed.

A float valve controls trough filling by using a buoyant float connected to a valve. When the water level drops, the float sinks and opens the valve, letting water in. As the water rises, the float rises with it and gradually closes the valve. At the set level, the valve shuts off and filling stops. Two ordinary causes of overflow are debris or mineral buildup preventing the valve from closing fully, and a misadjusted float set too high so the valve closes only after the trough is already overflowing.

Old school attendance registers can help historians reconstruct patterns of daily life that are often missing from official narratives. They show which children were present or absent, how regularly they attended, and sometimes why they missed school. From this, historians can infer seasonal labor demands, illness, bad weather, poverty, family responsibilities, migration, or local emergencies. Registers may also reveal differences by gender, age, neighborhood, or social class, helping researchers understand how education fitted into work, household routines, and community expectations. When studied across many years, they can show changes in schooling habits and public health.

A limitation is that attendance registers record only what the school chose to note. They rarely explain children’s experiences in detail, and absences may be misreported, incomplete, or shaped by teachers’ assumptions. Therefore, they are most useful when compared with other sources.

A siphon transfers water between two containers by utilizing gravity and atmospheric pressure to move liquid over an elevated barrier. The process begins when the tube is filled with water, creating a continuous column. Gravity pulls the water down the longer, descending leg of the tube toward the lower container. This downward movement creates a partial vacuum or reduced pressure at the top of the siphon. Atmospheric pressure pushing on the surface of the source water then forces more liquid up the shorter leg to fill this low-pressure zone, sustaining the flow.

The outlet must be positioned lower than the source water surface because the driving force is the weight difference between the water columns in the two legs. If the outlet were higher or level with the source, gravity would not pull the water down with sufficient force to overcome the upward lift required on the intake side. The net gravitational pull only exists when the exiting column is heavier than the rising column.

Air entering the tube interrupts this process by breaking the continuous liquid column. When air bubbles enter, they disrupt the cohesive chain of water molecules necessary for transmitting the suction effect. This break equalizes the pressure inside the tube with the outside atmosphere, stopping the pressure differential that drives the flow. Consequently, the siphon fails until the tube is re-primed and filled entirely with liquid again.
